title: Do the elderly prefer robotic care? - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: A survey of 4,314 Japanese aged 55-75 (Bertrand Achou et al.) finds 65% prefer a nursing home where robots and ICT deliver a substantial share of care, with willingness to pay about 8% above typical fees, strongest for mobility assistance.

insights.claim: In a survey of 4,314 Japanese individuals aged 55 to 75 choosing between otherwise identical nursing homes, 65 percent preferred the one where robots and ICT provide a substantial share of care.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Demand-side resistance to eldercare automation may be lower than assumed, supporting the addressable market for care robotics in aging societies.
insights.quote: A majority of respondents (65 percent) prefer nursing homes where robots and ICT are used.
insights.locator: Population aging and shortages of long-term

insights.claim: Average willingness to pay for a robot/ICT-assisted nursing home is about 8 percent above the typical nursing home fee.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: A positive price premium suggests care-robot adoption could be revenue-accretive for operators, not just a cost-cutting tool.
insights.quote: at 8 percent above the typical nursing home fee
insights.locator: Population aging and shortages of long-term

insights.claim: Acceptance of robots in eldercare varies by task: highest for mobility assistance, intermediate for monitoring, and lowest for communication.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Physical-assist robotics is the most commercially promising eldercare segment; social/companion robots face the most resistance.
insights.quote: It is highest for mobility assistance, intermediate for monitoring, and lowest for communication
insights.locator: Population aging and shortages of long-term

insights.claim: A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests the benefits of introducing robots and ICT in nursing care can greatly exceed the costs, particularly for mobility-aid robots.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Points to favorable economics for mobility-aid robots, though the authors frame it as only suggestive.
insights.locator: Population aging and shortages of long-term

insights.claim: Prior awareness of caregiving robots is positively associated with both acceptance and willingness to pay, implying information campaigns could raise adoption.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Awareness/marketing may be a lever for eldercare robot uptake.
insights.locator: Population aging and shortages of long-term

insights.claim: Population aging and shortages of long-term care workers are driving interest in caregiving robots and ICT in Japan.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Labor scarcity in eldercare is a structural demand driver for automation in aging economies.
insights.locator: Population aging and shortages of long-term
